newsitem.title: USA: G7 leaders say must do more to help world economy.
newsitem.headline: G7 leaders say must do more to help world economy.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

Leaders of the Group of Seven industrial nations welcomed signs of an improving world economy on Saturday but said more needed to be done to ensure that the good times continued and that everyone benefited.
In a draft of a statement to be issued later on Saturday, they also set out specific economic goals for their countries to help ensure that global expansion remains on track.

"We have been encouraged by the many positive indicators in our economies," the G7 countries -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- said. "But we still have work to do in our own economies."
Among the encouraging signs: low inflation, reduced budget deficits and solid growth. But unemployment remains high in some countries, particularly among the young.
"We face the challenge of ensuring that all, particularly our young people, can participate in growth and benefit from it."
In setting out specific goals for each nation, the G7 said the United States needed to guard against a resurgence of inflation and follow through with efforts to balance the government budget.
Japan must rely on domestic demand, not on exports, for faster economic growth and avoid a big rise in its trade surplus, they said.
France, Germany and Italy, all plagued by high unemployment, needed to restructure their economies to promote job creation. Britain must keep inflation in check and cut its budget deficit further.
Canada, the G7 said, has recently enjoyed faster economic growth that should reduce joblessness.

The leaders urged their finance ministers to work together and to cooperate closely in currency markets to help promote international monetary stability. They welcomed efforts by the European Union to forge a single currency but stressed that it must be backed up by sound economic policies.

The economic statement was to be issued after the G7 leaders met for about an hour later on Saturday to approve it. That was to be their only meeting in the three-day summit without Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who is using the time to talk to U.S. businessmen.

In the draft of their statement, the G7 leaders welcomed the new round of economic reforms that Russia has launched this year. "We fully agree with Russia's intention to pursue vigorously structural reforms to improve the investment environment, promote competition, fight crime and corruption and strengthen the social sector," the G7 said.
The group also called for increased lending and loan guarantees for Russia from the World Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

The G7 had tougher words for Russia's neighbor, Ukraine. Kiev needs to make progress now on reforming its economy if it wants to win financial help from other nations and international financial institutions, the draft said.
But the leaders did agree to give Ukraine $300 million to shore up the concrete sarcophagus covering the remains of the destroyed Chernobyl nuclear reactor.
The G7 leaders also said their countries were taking steps to help improve the workings of the international financial system and thus promote economic growth.
Those steps included increased sharing of information among financial market regulators and a concrete strategy for helping up-and-coming emerging market economies buttress their banking systems.
The G7 leaders said they intended to step up help to poor countries as well, provided they acted to overhaul their economies to give free markets greater rein.
"We remain committed, through this partnership...to meeting the interrelated challenges of eradicating deep-seated poverty...and promoting dignity," the group said.
It backed further action to reduce multilateral and bilateral debt owed by the world's poor nations.

Four countries -- Uganda, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast and Bolivia -- have already been lined up for debt relief under a joint initiative launched by the International Monetary Fund, World Bank and Paris Club of creditor nations.
